questions.q: What is the URL frontier in a web crawler?
options: The set of pages that have already been fetched and parsed
The queue of discovered URLs awaiting fetch, with priority and politeness scheduling
The index mapping content hashes back to their source URLs
The cache of hostnames the crawler has already resolved via DNS

questions.q: What does a site's robots.txt file communicate to a crawler?
options: A complete listing of every URL available on the site
API credentials the crawler must present to fetch pages
The cache TTLs that proxies should apply to the site's pages
Which paths a given crawler user-agent may or may not fetch

questions.q: What does politeness mean in crawler design?
options: Capping request rate per host so the crawler doesn't overwhelm servers
Honoring nofollow attributes when extracting outbound links
Fetching each site's pages only during its off-peak hours
Identifying the crawler honestly through its User-Agent header on every request

questions.q: How does a crawler detect that two fetched pages have identical content at scale?
options: Compare the full HTML byte-by-byte against every previously stored page
Compare page titles together with their content lengths
Compute a content hash and check membership in a seen-hash store
Compare rendered screenshots using perceptual image diffing

questions.q: Which structure is commonly used for the URL-seen test when memory is constrained?
options: A sorted append-only log scanned linearly on each lookup
An LRU cache in fetcher memory holding only the most recent million URLs
A per-host trie storing every previously crawled path
A Bloom filter, trading small false positives for compact memory

questions.q: What is the standard processing order once a crawler downloads a page?
options: Parse links, fetch them all immediately, deduplicate, then enqueue the survivors
Fetch, parse and extract links, normalize and dedupe them, then enqueue
Enqueue raw links, dedupe the frontier, then fetch and parse
Fetch, enqueue the page itself, parse later, normalize last

questions.q: Why is DNS resolution a notable crawler bottleneck, and what is the common fix?
options: Synchronous lookups per URL stall fetchers; a local DNS cache removes most of them
Public resolvers rate-limit crawlers after a few thousand queries
Resolvers return stale IP addresses for frequently updated sites
Every TCP handshake triggers repeated reverse PTR lookups

questions.q: What is a spider trap?
options: A page that blocks automated crawlers behind a CAPTCHA challenge before serving content
Malware served specifically to known crawler user agents
A site generating endless URL variations that can occupy a crawler indefinitely
A honeypot page that logs crawler IPs so the site can ban them

questions.q: How does a multi-threaded crawler enforce per-host politeness in its frontier?
options: A global FIFO with random worker pulls spreads hosts out naturally
Per-host queues, each assigned to one fetcher enforcing a delay between requests
Workers take an exclusive lock on the entire shared frontier during each page fetch
URLs are hashed by path so no two workers ever share a page

questions.q: How should a crawler consult robots.txt efficiently across billions of fetches?
options: Cache it per host with an expiry and check rules before every fetch
Fetch it once when a host is first seeded and never again
Check it only for URLs that appear to be behind authentication
Bake its rules into the frontier at discovery time and trust them forever

questions.q: Why must URLs be normalized before the URL-seen test runs?
options: Browsers refuse to open URLs that are not in normalized form
Normalization compresses frontier storage by roughly half
Hash functions used by the seen test require fixed-length canonical input strings
Equivalent URL variants would evade the seen test and be fetched repeatedly

questions.q: How should URLs be partitioned across machines in a distributed crawler?
options: Hash by full URL so the fetch load spreads as evenly as possible across all nodes
Round-robin each new URL to whichever node is least loaded
Partition by host so one node owns a site's politeness and robots state
Broadcast every URL to all nodes and deduplicate afterward

questions.q: How should a crawler decide when to revisit already-crawled pages?
options: Recrawl the entire corpus on a uniform weekly cycle
Recrawl only when sitemaps or RSS feeds explicitly announce a content change
Recrawl in original discovery order, oldest fetch first
Adapt per-page revisit rates from observed change frequency and importance

questions.q: Which combination of mechanisms defends a crawler against spider traps?
options: Depth and per-host page budgets plus URL-length caps to bound infinite spaces
Restricting the crawl to URLs listed in official sitemaps
Rendering JavaScript on every page to detect dynamic loops
Limiting the crawl to hosts that serve valid HTTPS certificates signed by trusted CAs

questions.q: A URL chain issues 30 consecutive redirects. What should the crawler do?
options: Keep following the chain until a terminal status code arrives
Retry the original URL from a different crawler node instead
Stop after a small hop limit and record the URL as failed
Switch to HEAD requests to resolve the chain more cheaply

questions.q: Two pages differ only in navigation boilerplate, so exact hashing misses the duplication. What is the standard fix?
options: Compare the depth and shape of each page's DOM tree
Locality-sensitive fingerprints like SimHash over shingles to catch near-duplicates
Strip all HTML tags and compare the remaining byte lengths
Crawl suspected mirrors from the same node and diff them directly

questions.q: In a crawler's URL-seen Bloom filter, what does a false positive cause?
options: A few never-crawled URLs are wrongly treated as seen and never fetched
Some URLs get crawled twice, wasting bandwidth on duplicates
The filter silently drops older entries whenever it becomes fully saturated
Frontier priority ordering degrades until it becomes random

questions.q: A high-priority host has millions of pages but demands a 10-second crawl delay. What follows?
options: Adding more fetcher threads will clear the host's backlog quickly
Priority queue weighting can override politeness for important hosts
Throughput on that host is capped by the delay, so its backlog drains slowly no matter the cluster size
Moving the host's queue to the fastest node restores throughput

questions.q: A fetcher node dies while holding thousands of frontier URLs. How does a robust design recover them?
options: The lost URLs get rediscovered organically through other pages' links
Peer nodes detect the death and immediately rehash all outstanding URLs
The URL-seen filter is rolled back to the last consistent checkpoint
Frontier leases expire and the dead node's URLs are reassigned, tolerating occasional refetches

questions.q: Headless-browser rendering costs 10-100x more than plain fetching. When is it justified in a crawl?
options: For every page, since modern sites all require JavaScript to render
Selectively, for valuable pages whose content appears only after client-side rendering
Never, because the server-sent HTML always contains the real content
Only for paginated listing pages that hide their content behind infinite scroll widgets
